summary.text: The proof groups divisors by their odd part and analyzes each resulting \(2\)-adic chain; because consecutive squared terms differ by a factor of \(4\), each chain contains at most one middle divisor, and it contains exactly one precisely when neither endpoint odd divisor is above the threshold. The involution \(u\mapsto \operatorname{oddpart}(n/u)\) pairs the threshold-exceeding odd divisors with a disjoint equally sized set of zero-contribution chains, yielding the required count.

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer. Write
\[
\mathcal O=\{d:d\mid n,\ d\text{ odd}\}
\]
for the set of odd divisors of \(n\), and write
\[
\mathcal M=\{d:d\mid n,\ n\le 2d^2\text{ and }d^2<2n\}
\]
for the set of middle divisors. Thus
\[
a(n)=|\mathcal O|-|\mathcal M|.
\]
The inequalities defining \(\mathcal M\) are precisely
\(\sqrt{n/2}\le d<\sqrt{2n}\).

We shall prove that
\[
|\mathcal M|=|\mathcal O|-2|\mathcal L|,
\qquad
\mathcal L:=\{u\in\mathcal O:2n<u^2\}.
\]
The desired formula then follows immediately, since \(\mathcal L\) is exactly the set of odd divisors greater than \(\sqrt{2n}\).

We use the odd part of an integer. For a positive integer \(d\), let \(v_2(d)\) be the exponent of \(2\) in its prime factorization and define
\[
\operatorname{op}(d)=\frac{d}{2^{v_2(d)}}.
\]
Then
\[
d=2^{v_2(d)}\operatorname{op}(d),
\]
\(\operatorname{op}(d)\) is odd, and \(\operatorname{op}(d)\mid d\). In particular, if \(d\mid n\), then \(\operatorname{op}(d)\mid n\). We will also repeatedly use the elementary facts that if \(u\) is odd, then
\[
\operatorname{op}(2^k u)=u,
\]
and that removing an odd divisor does not change the exponent of \(2\): if \(u\mid n\) is odd, then
\[
v_2(n/u)=v_2(n).
\]

Put
\[
a=v_2(n).
\]
For each \(u\in\mathcal O\), define
\[
T(u)=\operatorname{op}(n/u).
\]
Since \(u\) is odd and divides \(n\), the quotient \(n/u\) has 2-adic exponent \(a\). Hence there is an odd integer \(v=T(u)\) such that
\[
\frac nu=2^a v,
\qquad	ext{so that}\qquad
n=2^a u v. \tag{1}
\]
This shows that \(v\) is an odd divisor of \(n\), so \(T\) maps \(\mathcal O\) to itself. Moreover, dividing (1) by \(v\) gives
\[
\frac nv=2^a u.
\]
Taking odd parts yields
\[
T(v)=\operatorname{op}(n/v)=u.
\]
Thus
\[
T(T(u))=u \tag{2}
\]
for every \(u\in\mathcal O\). In particular, \(T\) is an involution and hence a bijection on \(\mathcal O\).

We now partition the middle divisors according to their odd parts. If \(d\mid n\), then \(v_2(d)\le v_2(n)=a\). Consequently, the divisors of \(n\) having odd part \(u\in\mathcal O\) are exactly
\[
2^k u\qquad(0\le k\le a).
\]
Indeed, every divisor with odd part \(u\) has this form, with \(k=v_2(d)\le a\). Conversely, if \(u\in\mathcal O\), equation (1) says \(n=2^a uT(u)\), so \(2^k u\mid n\) whenever \(k\le a\).

For \(u\in\mathcal O\), let \(c(u)\) be the number of integers \(k\) with \(0\le k\le a\) for which \(2^k u\) is a middle divisor. Explicitly,
\[
c(u)=\#\left\{k\in\{0,1,\ldots,a\}:
 n\le 2(2^k u)^2<4n\right\}. \tag{3}
\]
The upper inequality here is equivalent to \((2^ku)^2<2n\). Since every positive divisor has a unique odd part, the preceding partition gives
\[
|\mathcal M|=\sum_{u\in\mathcal O}c(u). \tag{4}
\]

We next determine every value \(c(u)\). First observe that
\[
2(2^k u)^2=2\cdot4^k u^2. \tag{5}
\]
The interval in (3) has multiplicative width \(4\). Therefore it contains at most one member of the geometric progression \(2u^2,2\cdot4u^2,2\cdot4^2u^2,\ldots\). More explicitly, if \(x<y\), then \(y\ge x+1\), and hence
\[
2\cdot4^y u^2\ge4\bigl(2\cdot4^x u^2\bigr).
\]
If the term with exponent \(x\) is at least \(n\), the term with exponent \(y\) is at least \(4n\), contrary to the strict upper bound in (3). Thus
\[
c(u)\le1. \tag{6}
\]

There are two ways in which \(c(u)\) can be zero.

First, if \(u\in\mathcal L\), so that \(u^2>2n\), then
\[
2(2^k u)^2\ge2u^2>4n
\]
for every \(k\ge0\). Thus no \(k\) satisfies (3), and
\[
c(u)=0\qquad(u\in\mathcal L). \tag{7}
\]

Second, suppose that
\[
T(u)^2>2n. \tag{8}
\]
Set \(v=T(u)\), so that \(n=2^a uv\). Since all quantities are positive, (8) becomes
\[
v^2>2^{a+1}uv,
\]
and cancellation of \(v\) gives
\[
v>2^{a+1}u. \tag{9}
\]
For every \(k\le a\), using (9),
\[
\begin{aligned}
2(2^k u)^2
&=2\cdot4^k u^2\\
&\le2\cdot4^a u^2\\
&=(2^{a+1}u)(2^a u)\\
&<v(2^a u)=n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the lower inequality in (3) fails for every allowed \(k\), and hence
\[
c(u)=0\qquad\text{if }T(u)^2>2n. \tag{10}
\]
By the involution property (2), the set of \(u\) satisfying (8) is exactly \(T(\mathcal L)\).

We now prove that these are the only zero-contribution cases. Suppose
\[
u^2\le2n
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
T(u)^2\le2n. \tag{11}
\]
Because \(u\) is odd, \(u^2\) is odd, whereas \(2n\) is even. Therefore equality is impossible in the first inequality of (11), and in fact
\[
u^2<2n.
\]
Consequently, with \(X=2u^2\), we have
\[
0<X<4n. \tag{12}
\]

Consider the sequence \(X,4X,4^2X,\ldots\). Some term is at least \(n\), since it grows without bound. Let \(k\) be the least nonnegative integer such that
\[
n\le4^kX. \tag{13}
\]
This least term also satisfies
\[
4^kX<4n. \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, if \(k=0\), this is (12). If \(k>0\), minimality gives \(4^{k-1}X<n\), and multiplying by \(4\) gives \(4^kX<4n\). Since \(X=2u^2\), (13) and (14) say
\[
n\le2(2^ku)^2<4n. \tag{15}
\]
It remains only to show that this \(k\) lies in the permissible range, namely \(k\le a\).

Again put \(v=T(u)\), so \(n=2^auv\). If instead \(k\ge a+1\), then (14) would imply
\[
2\cdot4^{a+1}u^2
\le 2\cdot4^ku^2
<4n=4\cdot2^auv. \tag{16}
\]
Canceling the positive common factor \(2^{a+2}u\) in (16) gives
\[
2^{a+1}u<v.
\]
Multiplying this strict inequality by the positive integer \(v\) yields
\[
2^{a+1}uv<v^2.
\]
But \(2^{a+1}uv=2n\), so this says \(2n<v^2\), contradicting the second inequality in (11). Therefore \(k\le a\). The exponent \(k\) found above is consequently counted in (3), so \(c(u)\ge1\). Together with (6), this proves
\[
c(u)=1
\quad\text{whenever}\quad
u^2\le2n\text{ and }T(u)^2\le2n. \tag{17}
\]

Combining (7), (10), and (17), we have completely classified the chains:
\[
c(u)=
\begin{cases}
0,&u\in\mathcal L\cup T(\mathcal L),\\
1,&u\in\mathcal O\setminus\bigl(\mathcal L\cup T(\mathcal L)\bigr).
\end{cases} \tag{18}
\]

It remains to count the two exceptional classes. Because \(T\) is an involution, it is injective, so
\[
|T(\mathcal L)|=|\mathcal L|. \tag{19}
\]
Moreover, \(\mathcal L\) and \(T(\mathcal L)\) are disjoint. To see this, suppose for contradiction that \(x=T(u)\in\mathcal L\) for some \(u\in\mathcal L\). Since \(u^2>2n\) and \(x^2>2n\), multiplication gives
\[
(ux)^2=u^2x^2>4n^2. \tag{20}
\]
On the other hand, equation (1) gives \(n=2^aux\), and hence \(ux\le n\). Squaring gives
\[
(ux)^2\le n^2,
\]
contradicting (20). Thus
\[
\mathcal L\cap T(\mathcal L)=\varnothing. \tag{21}
\]
Therefore
\[
|\mathcal L\cup T(\mathcal L)|=2|\mathcal L|. \tag{22}
\]

Now sum (18) over \(u\in\mathcal O\). Using (4) and (22), we obtain
\[
|\mathcal M|
=\sum_{u\in\mathcal O}c(u)
=\left|\mathcal O\setminus\bigl(\mathcal L\cup T(\mathcal L)\bigr)\right|
=|\mathcal O|-2|\mathcal L|. \tag{23}
\]
In particular, (22) also shows directly that \(2|\mathcal L|\le|\mathcal O|\), so the subtraction in (23) is ordinary nonnegative integer subtraction.

Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
&=|\mathcal O|-|\mathcal M|\\
&=|\mathcal O|-\bigl(|\mathcal O|-2|\mathcal L|\bigr)\\
&=2|\mathcal L|.
\end{aligned}
\]
For a positive divisor \(d\), the condition \(2n<d^2\) is equivalent to \(d>\sqrt{2n}\). Hence \(\mathcal L\) is precisely the set of odd divisors of \(n\) greater than \(\sqrt{2n}\). Thus, for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)\) is twice the number of odd divisors of \(n\) greater than \(\sqrt{2n}\), as claimed.
